content: The updated recommendations from the Immunization Practices Advisory Committee (ACIP) on measles prevention incorporate the latest data on vaccine effectiveness and efforts to eliminate measles. The Schwarz strain of the live, attenuated measles vaccine was introduced in 1965, followed by the Moraten strain in 1968. These vaccines, which are more attenuated than the Edmonston B vaccine, cause fewer adverse reactions while maintaining equivalent efficacy. The Moraten vaccine is currently the standard in the United States. The recommended age for measles vaccination has evolved over time. Initially set at 9 months in 1963, it was increased to 12 months in 1965 and then to 15 months in 1976, based on evidence of improved vaccine efficacy at older ages. While vaccination at 15 months is optimal, administration as early as 12 months (on or after the first birthday) is considered sufficient to establish immunity. Children vaccinated between 12 and 14 months are not routinely revaccinated. Since the introduction of the measles vaccine in 1963, collaborative vaccination efforts by medical and public health organizations have led to a 98%-99% reduction in reported measles cases in the United States. During the late 1960s and early 1970s, annual reported cases dropped to between 22,000 and 75,000, with significant declines in incidence across all age groups. The most substantial reduction occurred in children under 10 years old, while older children experienced a less dramatic decrease. In 1978, a Measles Elimination Program was launched with the goal of eradicating indigenous measles in the United States by October 1, 1982. This program focused on three key components: achieving and maintaining high levels of immunity, effective disease surveillance, and aggressive outbreak control. These efforts further reduced annual reported measles cases. Measles (rubeola) is a potentially severe disease often complicated by middle ear infections or bronchopneumonia. Encephalitis occurs in approximately 1 in 2,000 reported cases, frequently resulting in permanent brain damage or mental retardation. Death, primarily due to respiratory or neurological complications, occurs in 1 in 3,000 cases, with higher risk in infants and adults compared to children and adolescents. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare but fatal central nervous system infection associated with the measles virus, has nearly disappeared in the United States due to widespread vaccination. Contracting measles during pregnancy increases the risk of complications such as premature labor, spontaneous abortion, and low birth weight. Although one study suggested a potential link between first-trimester measles infection and congenital malformations, this has not been confirmed. Before the availability of the measles vaccine, over 400,000 cases were reported annually in the United States. Both the type of measles vaccine and the recommended age for vaccination have changed since 1963, when both inactivated and live attenuated vaccines (Edmonston B strain) were licensed. The inactivated vaccine was used until 1967, and the Edmonston B vaccine until 1972. A more attenuated live vaccine was introduced in 1965. Despite significant progress in reducing measles incidence, the goal of eliminating indigenous measles has not been fully achieved. Challenges include incomplete implementation of vaccination strategies and vaccine failures, which may be primary (failure to develop an adequate immune response) or secondary (waning immunity over time). Some cases of vaccine failure may be due to inaccurate vaccination records. The measles vaccine is at least 95% effective in children vaccinated at 15 months of age, though efficacy may be slightly lower in those vaccinated between 12 and 14 months due to the persistence of maternal antibodies. Imported measles cases, though accounting for only 2% of cases, have triggered outbreaks and may contribute to more cases than surveillance data suggests. To address these challenges, the ACIP has reviewed current measles epidemiology and elimination strategies. While no changes to routine vaccination policies are recommended at this time, careful monitoring and analysis of measles trends are essential to guide future modifications. The live measles virus vaccine, prepared in chick embryo cell culture, is available in monovalent form or in combination vaccines such as measles-rubella (MR) and measles-mumps-rubella (MMR). The MMR vaccine is preferred for routine use, and combination vaccines should be administered when recipients are likely to be susceptible to rubella and/or mumps in addition to measles. Revaccination poses no harm to individuals already immune to any of the vaccine components. The vaccine induces a mild or inapparent non-communicable infection, with antibodies developing in at least 95% of susceptible children vaccinated at 15 months. Long-term data indicate durable protection, despite lower antibody titers compared to natural infection. Proper storage and handling of the vaccine are critical to maintaining its efficacy. The vaccine must be stored at temperatures of 2°C to 8°C (35°F to 46°F) and protected from light. Improperly stored vaccine may fail to provide protection. Individuals are considered immune to measles if they have documentation of adequate immunization with live vaccine on or after their first birthday, physician-diagnosed measles, or laboratory evidence of immunity. Routine serologic screening to determine immunity is not recommended. A single dose of live measles vaccine, administered subcutaneously, is sufficient if given on or after the first birthday. Vaccination is particularly important for children at 15 months of age to prevent exposure in high-risk environments such as daycare centers. Infants as young as 6 months may be vaccinated in outbreak settings, but they should be revaccinated at 15 months due to lower seroconversion rates. Revaccination is recommended for individuals vaccinated with inactivated vaccine, vaccine of unknown type, or live vaccine administered before the first birthday. Those vaccinated between 12 and 14 months generally do not require routine revaccination, but it may be considered in outbreak settings. Individuals exposed to measles should receive live vaccine within 72 hours of exposure or immune globulin (IG) within 6 days if vaccination is contraindicated. The measles vaccine has an excellent safety record, with over 160 million doses distributed in the United States by 1986. Adverse reactions are rare and typically mild, including fever and transient rash. Severe neurologic conditions such as encephalitis occur at a rate of less than one case per million doses. Febrile seizures following vaccination are uncommon and do not increase the risk of epilepsy or other neurologic disorders. Live measles vaccine should not be administered to pregnant women or individuals with severe immunodeficiency. Vaccination of close contacts can reduce the risk of exposure for immunocompromised individuals. Simultaneous administration of MMR, oral polio vaccine (OPV), and diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP) vaccine is safe and effective. Ongoing vaccination programs targeting children at 15 months of age are essential to reducing measles incidence. Immunization efforts must be maintained to achieve and sustain high levels of population immunity.
